sources.news_title: Life in the peace lane
sources.text:
Life in the peace lane
Donald the Dove reflects on the ongoing importance of diplomacy:
President Trump told Axios on Thursday that he’s seriously considering restarting major combat operations in Iran — including strikes that would be bigger than the ones carried out during Operation Epic Fury.
Why it matters: In a brief interview, Trump acknowledged that such a decision would have consequences and stressed he hasn’t made a determination yet.
Trump didn’t give a deadline for his decision. Two other U.S. officials confirmed no call has been made and no new orders have been given to the military.
The current escalation has caused oil prices to eclipse $100 per barrel. A return to all-out war is highly unpopular in the U.S.
What he’s saying: “I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before. I am close to making a decision. We are all set for it,” the president said.
Trump said Israel “would join in two minutes if I ask them to,” but added that “we don’t need anybody” to launch a new operation against Iran.
He also said there would be “consequences” for Israel joining the strikes, hinting at Iranian retaliation against Israel.
The big picture: Trump said the Iranians “want to negotiate” but are not ready to make a deal at the moment.
“They haven’t received enough pain yet,” he said.
I’m beginning to think that Trump criticizing the Iraq War for not being brutal and rapacious enough was not, in fact, good evidence that he opposed military adventurism.

sources.news_title: Trump demands Saudi Arabia normalize relations with Israel for nuclear deal | Honolulu Star-Advertiser
sources.text:
Trump demands Saudi Arabia normalize relations with Israel for nuclear deal
WASHINGTON >> A day after the United States signed a landmark nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia, President Donald Trump added a new condition to the sale of nuclear reactors to the kingdom, declaring that the entire arrangement now depends on the Saudi willingness to establish diplomatic relations with Israel.
The deal “is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords,” Trump said in a post on his social media site, referring to a series of agreements that normalized relations between Israel and other states, including Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates.
There was no mention of any such condition in the administration’s announcement that the deal had been signed Wednesday, and the text of the deal has not been released. But Trump’s social media post put the agreement’s immediate future in doubt. The Saudi government has made clear it has no intention of recognizing Israel without creating a pathway toward the creation of a Palestinian state.
Trump’s post did not address the Saudi government’s conditions for establishing diplomatic ties with Israel. Saudi officials have not responded to repeated requests for comment.
When a reporter pressed Karoline Leavitt, the White House spokesperson, on why the condition was not mentioned in the announcement of the deal Wednesday, she said the president was the “final dealmaker” and had mentioned the need for Saudi Arabia to join the accords “on numerous occasions.”
She was definitive on the president’s terms. “If they don’t join the Abraham Accords, the deal is off,” Leavitt said.

In linking the deal to diplomatic recognition of Israel, Trump is veering back to the plan that President Joe Biden attempted in the first years of his administration, making nuclear cooperation part of a larger diplomatic understanding that changes the dynamics of the Middle East. But the plan fell apart after the Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attacks on Israel by Hamas, and Trump later divorced the nuclear agreement from the diplomatic effort.
He has now reversed himself, but only after his energy secretary, Chris Wright, signed the deal with Saudi Arabia’s energy minister. Wright indicated that the deal would now be sent to Congress for review, but presumably Trump could hold up its transmission while he argues with the Saudis over the new condition.
Not surprisingly, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel warmly greeted Trump’s demand that the Saudis normalize relations with Israel. “The joint American and Israeli military action against the genocidal regime in Tehran and Israel’s crushing of Iran’s terror axis have created the possibility to expand the circle of peace,” he said in a statement. “As President Trump has said, Saudi Arabia’s joining of the Abraham Accords would be an historic leap forward for peace in the Middle East.”
Saudi Arabia’s Center for International Communication did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Trump’s demand.
Trump also asserted that the terms of the deal would not allow Saudi Arabia to enrich its own nuclear material, offering no further explanation. While the agreement has not been made public, officials have described it very differently, saying that it allows for a two-year study period, during which Saudi and U.S. officials will determine if there is a viable economic path for the kingdom to enrich nuclear fuel. The U.S. could block that move for a number of years, according to officials familiar with the arrangement, but not permanently.
Trump argued otherwise.
“There will be no enrichment of material,” he stated, adding that the United States “is not opposed to Civil (Non-Enriched) Nuclear Facilities.”
The potential that Saudi Arabia could make its own fuel — and the risk that some of it could be diverted to a nuclear weapons project in the future — lies at the core of criticism of the deal. But the country’s de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, is unlikely to give up the right to enrich or agree to the most intrusive international inspections that more than 140 other nations have already signed.
Trump’s statement comes after Israeli leaders voiced concerns over the emerging deal, worrying that it could fuel a regional arms race and that the implication was of Israel being sidestepped in the process.
But Trump’s newly stated condition could create a roadblock to the deal itself, as Saudi officials have repeatedly stated that they will not recognize Israel without a pathway toward a Palestinian state.
Trump has previously pushed to expand the Abraham Accords, agreements he began brokering during his first term. The first, between Israel and Bahrain and the UAE, were announced in 2020. Since then, Morocco and Sudan have joined the pact.

US says Saudi nuclear deal off without Israel recognition
- US President Trump said the Saudi nuclear deal depends on Saudi Arabia normalising relations with Israel by joining the Abraham Accords.
- The deal allows Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium and build reactors using US technology, but with strict nonproliferation conditions and a review period.
- Israel welcomed the condition linking the deal to peace efforts, while Saudi Arabia has yet to respond or agree to normalisation.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump conditioned a civilian nuclear cooperation deal with Saudi Arabia on July 23 on Riyadh normalising relations with Israel, an action the kingdom has so far refused to take.
Trump said the deal would take effect only if Saudi Arabia joined the US-brokered Abraham Accords under which several Arab states established ties with Israel.
The kingdom has long rejected joining the accords absent a pathway towards Palestinian statehood.
Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, said Trump had spoken with Gulf and Arab allies many times about pegging the deal to the Abraham Accords and that if the kingdom does not join them “the deal is off.”
The US and Saudi Arabia announced the agreement on July 22 allowing Riyadh to enrich uranium and build nuclear reactors using US technology without the snap UN inspections Washington has demanded of Iran.
Trump ties Saudi nuclear deal to Abraham Accords
In a post on Truth Social on July 23, Trump wrote: “The Civil Nuclear Deal (There will be no enrichment of material!)... pertains only to non-military use such as the ones that Iran and UAE (and others) already have, will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords.”
“The United States is not opposed to Civil (Non-Enriched) Nuclear Facilities,” Trump said.
The US Congress will have 90 session days to review the deal before it goes into force. There would also be a two-year feasibility study on the enrichment part of the agreement.
The Saudi Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment on Trump’s post.
Saudi Arabia said before Trump pegged the deal to the Abraham Accords that the agreement supports efforts to diversify energy sources, and includes the “highest international standards” of nuclear safety, security and nonproliferation.
‘We’ll continue to talk,’ press secretary says
“We’ll continue to talk with our Saudi counterparts to get the deal finalized and hopefully see them joining Abraham Accords very soon,” Leavitt told reporters at the White House.
Leavitt said she did not believe Trump had spoken with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman since his post, but it was something he had raised in previous conversations.
The United Arab Emirates and Bahrain signed the Abraham Accords during Trump’s first term in 2020, breaking a longstanding taboo to become the first Arab states to recognise Israel in a quarter century. Morocco and Sudan followed suit.
Israel, which feared the Saudi deal could ignite a Middle East arms race, welcomed the condition on July 23.
“Saudi Arabia’s joining of the Abraham Accords would be an historic leap forward for peace in the Middle East,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said in a statement.
Leavitt said she did not know if Netanyahu had requested that the deal be contingent on the wider accords. “Not to my knowledge, no,” she told reporters.
On July 22, the Trump administration said the civil nuclear deal abides by nonproliferation agreements in the US Atomic Energy Act, which are among the world’s strongest.
The deal would let Saudi Arabia enrich uranium and reprocess nuclear waste, both of which are potential pathways to a nuclear weapon. The UAE agreed to forgo both when it signed a similar deal with the US in 2009.
It was unclear what Trump meant in his social media post when he said there would be no nuclear enrichment under the agreement. It was not immediately clear if that was a specific reference to the highly enriched uranium used in weapons. Weapons-grade uranium is enriched to about 90 per cent while fuel for nuclear reactors is enriched to up to 6 per cent.
The UN’s International Atomic Energy Agency said it was awaiting a request from Washington and Riyadh to implement verification measures under the agreement before seeking authorisation from its board of governors. REUTERS

sources.news_title: What happens next with the US-Saudi nuclear deal?
sources.text:
What happens next with the US-Saudi nuclear deal?
US-Saudi nuclear deal faces a hurdle as Trump links it to Riyadh normalising ties with Israel
A US-Saudi deal to establish a civilian nuclear programme in the Gulf country looked like a triumph for the kingdom, but just hours after its announcement, President Donald Trump revealed a major caveat.
With Trump saying the deal is "totally subject" to Saudi Arabia normalising relations with Israel, here is a rundown of where things stand.
Has Trump already killed the deal?
After signing the agreement, Saudi Arabia appeared to score a diplomatic victory and be on the brink of securing its years-long dream of launching a civilian nuclear energy programme.
But just hours after Saudi Arabia signed the landmark agreement, Trump announced a new caveat to the deal via Truth Social.
The nuclear agreement "will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords", Trump wrote.
That could be a nonstarter for Saudi Arabia, which insists that there can be no ties with Israel unless a pathway to establish a Palestinian state is hammered out first.
"If DC tries to force normalisation on Riyadh, it's not likely to work out very well," H.A. Hellyer, an analyst at the Royal United Services Institute in London, told AFP.
"Israel has the most toxic brand it has ever had. Would Saudi decide to do a complete 180 on what it has declared for the past three years, or thirty years? Quite dubious."
Trump's latest curveball is potentially a stunning reversal for the kingdom's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who was on the verge of cementing a major diplomatic and economic triumph for the kingdom.
Embracing nuclear technology is in line with Saudi policy to address the rapid increase in energy demand in the kingdom while reducing "the reliance on hydrocarbons in order to use petroleum for higher value purposes and export", according to the energy ministry.
If approved by Congress, the deal would also likely provide an economic windfall for US energy companies and further undergird Riyadh's ironclad ties with the US.
"The alternative was not a Saudi Arabia without nuclear ambitions, it was a Saudi nuclear programme anchored in Russian or Chinese supply chains, with no American visibility, no commercial foothold for Westinghouse and no structural leverage," Hesham Alghannam, a Saudi security analyst and researcher, told AFP.
Where do things stand now?
While the actual text of the deal has yet to be released, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisted on Thursday that appropriate safeguards against nuclear proliferation would be cemented in the agreement.
"We will ensure that in order to get congressional approval, we're going to need to have those safeguards in place," Rubio said on the sidelines of a summit in Manila.
Read More: Trump says US-Saudi nuclear deal conditional on country joining Abraham Accords
But there is likely to be harsh criticism of the agreement, along with worries that the move could further destabilise a region already upended by years of war.
Israel, however, is likely celebrating Trump's latest announcement.
For years, the US had sought to condition a nuclear deal and a US-Saudi defence pact on normalisation with Israel, and Trump has all but ensured that this policy will remain in place.
And then there's Iran.
The announcement comes as the US is fighting a war with Iran that began in large part over concerns about Tehran's nuclear programme and enrichment levels of its uranium stockpiles, still a key point of contention in now-stalled peace talks.
The Wall Street Journal had earlier reported that one provision in the US-Saudi deal would potentially see US companies build a uranium enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia.
However, Trump appeared to pour cold water on the idea, saying in his Truth Social post: "There will be no enrichment of material!"
The US Energy Department made no mention of such a provision and did not offer comment when asked about it by AFP.
What does it mean for the region?
For decades, US policymakers have worried about the potential consequences of the spread of nuclear technology and weaponisation of energy programmes, fearing it could spur arms races in places like the Middle East.
For some analysts, the deal is part of a new emerging security context that has begun forming in the wake of the ongoing war with Iran.
"The broader signal is that the post-war Middle East is generating a new set of rules on nuclear cooperation, security guarantees and great-power competition simultaneously," Alghannam said.

sources.news_title: Trump’s Saudi Nuclear Deal Reversal Is Right in Line With the Rest of His Foreign Policy
sources.text:
Sign up for the Slatest to get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.
It’s becoming a standard feature of Donald Trump’s second presidency: He makes an announcement or sets in motion a new, significant policy—then he utters a remark or posts a caveat on social media, and the ship of state is cast into chaos, national policy rendered uncertain, the words and deeds of the world’s most powerful leader reduced to unreliable gibberish.
On Wednesday, the secretary of energy signed an agreement by which the United States would supply Saudi Arabia with nuclear energy technology. This was a very big deal. The Saudis have been seeking such a deal for many years. It could wean the kingdom away from its reliance on oil—but it could also lay the foundations for a Saudi nuclear weapon, which in turn could spur others in the region to build nuclear arsenals as well. And unlike similar agreements that the U.S. had struck with dozens of other countries, this one seemed unconditional. Saudi Arabia long ago signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, but it did not sign the NPT’s Additional Protocol, which allows international agents to conduct on-site inspections of reactors to verify that its operators aren’t converting the fuel for military purposes.
Israelis of all political stripes, taken by surprise by the deal, voiced alarm, fearing that this would inevitably lead to a Saudi nuclear weapon. Previous talks over a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia hinged on normalization with Israel and there appeared to be no such condition for this deal. As I wrote on Wednesday, the concern in Israel over the Saudi deal seemed to indicate just how much favor Israel has lost in the United States in recent years.
Then, on Thursday, at 7:52 a.m., Trump posted on social media that the deal “is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords.” These accords involve Arab or Muslim countries normalizing relations with Israel. (Negotiated in the final months of Trump’s first term, the initial signatories were Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates, followed by Morocco, Sudan, and Kazakhstan.) Trump’s post immediately threw a huge wrench into the deal. The Saudis have repeatedly said that they will not normalize relations with Israel unless Israel resumes talks toward creating a Palestinian state. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has repeatedly said he opposes such a state and has rejected even holding talks on the subject. (Since Hamas’ attack on Oct. 7, 2023, a strong majority of the Israeli population is skeptical of any peace deal with Palestinians.)
In other words, Trump’s new condition—which was not included in the deal negotiated earlier this week by Secretary of Energy Chris Wright and his Saudi counterpart—pretty much scuttles the deal. As one indicator of this, on Thursday, Netanyahu praised Trump’s social media post.
This may not be the end of the story. It is worth noting that President Joe Biden tried to negotiate a nuclear deal with the Saudis but made the deal dependent on the Saudis’ normalizing relations with Israel—which the Saudis rejected. Will Trump change his mind and once again loosen the deal’s terms once he realizes that he is now taking the same position as Biden, whom he incessantly lampoons as “sleepy Joe” and “the worst president” in American history?
It is also unclear where Trump’s equivocation leaves U.S.–Israel relations. The alliance has genuinely soured in recent months. Trump has steadily lost trust in Netanyahu, once shouting obscenities at him for restarting the war on Hezbollah in Lebanon just as Trump was seeking a ceasefire in Iran. At the same time, American public opinion has turned against Israel for its deadly attacks against Palestinian civilians in Gaza and the West Bank; this has led to growing numbers in Congress voting to cut off all military aid to Israel—a proposition that would have been unimaginable even a year ago.
Trump’s social media post suggests the alliance isn’t finished. But it leaves open many questions about Trump’s relationship with the Saudis, with Israel, and with the nuclear power industry, whose ailing fortunes the deal would have greatly boosted.
It’s unclear why or how Trump changed his mind, if he did change his mind. Did he know, or just not notice, that the agreement signed by his energy secretary contained no Saudi concessions on Israel (or much else)? If so, it’s unsettling that a Cabinet secretary can sign a historic contract with a foreign power without the president’s prior endorsement or full understanding. The next time Wright or any other Cabinet secretary pens an agreement abroad (or makes any sort of promise), the foreign government and everyone else in the world would have good reason to wonder whether the secretary is reflecting the president’s views—and whether those views might change a day or two later. If you’re an American ally (or adversary or something in between), it’s basically impossible to believe anything our president says at this point, or to view us as anything close to a reliable partner.
There’s something else very jolting about Trump’s social media post Thursday morning. Some of its language suggests that, despite several briefings, he completely misunderstands the subject of uranium enrichment—crucial to any negotiation with Iran. Toward the end of the post, he writes: “The United States is not opposed to Civil (Non-Enriched) Nuclear Facilities.” He seems to think that, in the context of nuclear facilities, “civil” is synonymous with “non-enriched.” In other words, he seems to think that if the facility is enriching uranium at all, it is by definition military—i.e., its purpose is to build nuclear weapons.
This simply isn’t true. By common understanding, uranium must be enriched to a level of 20 percent purity to be deemed “highly enriched” and 90 percent to be “weapons-grade.” (It is also generally recognized that it doesn’t take much time to go from 60 percent—the level that Iran’s enrichment had reached—to 90 percent.) During negotiations in February, Iran proposed restricting its enrichment to 3.67 percent and suspending all enrichment for five years. Trump rejected the idea because he wanted no enrichment, and so he started the war.
If Trump had known that 3.67 percent enrichment is nowhere near the level needed to build a bomb, might he have continued the talks with Iran and refrained from the bombing campaign, which has killed thousands of people and completely destabilized the global economy? Or did he reject the idea because he was told that 3.67 percent was the same level of enrichment allowed by the Iran nuclear deal signed by President Barack Obama and five other leaders back in 2015—the deal that Trump scuttled three years later, calling it the worst deal ever negotiated?
To put it another way: Is Trump’s position on enrichment driven by ignorance of the subject or by hatred of the Democratic presidents who came before him? Either way, it’s tragic that this is America’s leader at such a precarious moment in history.

sources.news_title: 'Tweets don’t overturn signed agreements': Trump just learned the limits of his power
sources.text:
On Wednesday, the bombshell announcement that the Trump administration will allow Saudi Arabia to launch a nuclear program drew widespread condemnation from critics asserting it would fuel the proliferation of nuclear weapons. Then Thursday morning, President Donald Trump attempted to backpedal, claiming the deal was conditional on the Saudis normalizing relations with Israel. But according to sources, he’s about to learn the limits of his social media power. 
This is according to veteran foreign affairs reporter Lauren Rozen, who on Thursday said that when asked about the new conditions Trump is trying to add to the deal, a Saudi source told her that “it was signed,” so there was “nothing to renegotiate,” adding, “Tweets don’t overturn signed agreements.”
Trump’s post in question made a number of assertions that appear to conflict with reality. According to Trump, “The Civil Nuclear Deal (There will be no enrichment of material!) being made between the United States Department of Energy and Saudi Arabia, which pertains only to non-military use such as the ones that Iran and UAE (and others) already have, will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords. The United States is not opposed to Civil (Non-Enriched) Nuclear Facilities.”
First of all, Trump’s claim that there would be “no enrichment” not only clashes with how experts have assessed the deal, but is outright impossible. While the agreement theoretically focuses on the U.S. bringing nuclear power technology to Saudi Arabia, according to Yoel Guzansky, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Israel, the plan appeared to let Saudi Arabia enrich its own nuclear fuel in-country. Said Guzansky, "Saudi insistence on enrichment in Saudi Arabia ... was the thing that got [previous] negotiations stuck and U.S. administrations, one after another, did not permit enrichment.” What’s more, all nuclear facilities — whether for energy or weapons — rely on enriched material. In other words, Trump’s insistence that there will be “non-enriched” facilities is nonsensical.
But perhaps most importantly of all, as Rozen’s source pointed out, Trump’s post has no legal weight. A number of experts have agreed. 
“The U.S.-Saudi nuclear deal was signed yesterday,” said Axios Global Affairs Correspondent Barak Ravid. “But at the current time, Saudi Arabia signing a peace deal with Israel doesn't seem like a realistic near-term scenario.”
“Most normal countries go by what the actual text of an agreement says,” posted former U.S. Ambassador to Israel Dan Shapiro. “And while Trump is willing to screw the countries he doesn't like (Canada, e.g.) by violating signed agreements, my bet is today’s outburst is momentary spin to respond to criticism the deal is getting, and then the deal goes forward as written because it is a country he likes (and who knows who is getting cut in on the reactor deals).”
Center for International Policy Senior Fellow Sina Toossi warned that there could be wider diplomatic implications for the president’s attempt at rule by social media, declaring, “Trump has spent years destroying America's negotiating credibility. When even close partners have to wonder whether a signed agreement will survive his next post, diplomacy becomes exponentially harder.”

sources.news_title: Trump ties Saudi nuclear deal on Abraham accords
sources.text:
ALBAWABA- US President Donald Trump said Thursday that the newly signed civilian nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia will take effect only if Riyadh joins the Abraham Accords, while ruling out any Saudi uranium enrichment under the deal.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said the agreement is "totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords" and stressed that the nuclear program would be strictly for peaceful purposes.
"There will be no enrichment of material!" Trump wrote, adding that the United States supports civilian nuclear energy without uranium enrichment, citing countries that operate nuclear power plants using imported fuel.
Trump's remarks clarify the terms of the agreement signed on July 22 by US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman. The accord, concluded under Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, establishes a framework for up to 30 years of civilian nuclear cooperation and positions American companies to play a leading role in developing Saudi Arabia's nuclear energy infrastructure.
The agreement focuses on peaceful nuclear energy production, with US oversight intended to ensure compliance with non-proliferation commitments. While earlier reports suggested the possibility of a joint US-Saudi study on domestic nuclear fuel production, Trump's latest statement makes clear that uranium enrichment will not be permitted under the agreement.
White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt reinforced the administration's position, saying the agreement would not proceed unless Saudi Arabia joins the Abraham Accords. She described the deal as consistent with Trump's "America First" agenda, arguing that it would create jobs for US companies, expand American energy exports, and strengthen strategic partnerships while maintaining strict non-proliferation standards.
The agreement marks a significant step in US-Saudi relations but also highlights Washington's contrasting approach toward Iran's nuclear program. While the United States is prepared to support Saudi Arabia's civilian nuclear ambitions under strict conditions, it continues to oppose Iran's uranium enrichment activities, citing concerns that they could contribute to the development of nuclear weapons.
The deal also adds a diplomatic dimension to US efforts to expand the Abraham Accords, the normalization framework launched during Trump's first administration between Israel and several Arab states. Saudi Arabia has previously linked normalization with Israel to progress on the Palestinian issue and broader security guarantees, leaving the timeline for any agreement uncertain.
The nuclear accord remains subject to congressional review before entering into force, with lawmakers expected to closely examine its non-proliferation provisions and strategic implications for the Middle East.

sources.news_title: Trump says US-Saudi nuclear deal subject to Israeli normalization
sources.text:
The U.S. civilian nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia is contingent on normalization with Israel and would not allow for the production of atomic weapons, President Donald Trump wrote Thursday in a post on Truth Social.
The deal signed Wednesday by U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman had set off alarm bells in Jerusalem and Washington.
Critics feared the deal lacks appropriate oversight to prevent the plants from enriching weapons-grade uranium and to reprocess spent nuclear fuel. The statement announcing the deal, for instance, does not say it would require Saudi Arabia to abide by the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty’s Additional Protocol, which allows for snap inspections.
Washington’s and Saudi Arabia’s announcement of the deal on Wednesday also did not mention a normalization agreement with Israel.
A U.S.-Saudi civilian nuclear deal had been one of the key incentives Washington and Jerusalem had hoped would sway the Kingdom to normalize ties with Israel under the Biden administration. Those efforts were scuttled by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on October 7, 2023, that sparked the Gaza war.
Trump pushed back at criticism of the deal on Thursday, stating: “The Civil Nuclear Deal (There will be no enrichment of material!) being made between the United States Department of Energy and Saudi Arabia, which pertains only to non-military use such as the ones that Iran and UAE (and others) already have, will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords.”
Trump pushed back against reports Wednesday that the deal would allow enrichment of fissile material. “The United States is not opposed to Civil (Non-Enriched) Nuclear Facilities,” he said.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office notably only referred to the prospect of normalization, and not the nuclear deal, in a statement about the kingdom issued Thursday.
“The joint American and Israeli military action against the genocidal regime in Tehran and Israel’s crushing of Iran’s terror axis have created the possibility to expand the circle of peace,” Netanyahu’s office said. “Saudi Arabia’s joining of the Abraham Accords would be an historic leap forward for peace in the Middle East.”
Netanyahu’s colleagues were more critical.
“A civilian nuclear program isn’t what Israel wants to see, but it seems that it doesn’t have the ability to prevent it,” Agriculture Minister Avi Dichter, who formerly headed Israel’s Security Agency, wrote on X.
Laura Rozen, an independent journalist covering foreign policy, quoted a Saudi source as saying the deal was not subject to alteration.
“It was signed. So nothing to renegotiate,” Rozen quoted the source as saying. “Tweets don’t overturn signed agreements.”
Netanyahu has long sought a normalization deal with Saudi Arabia and to include it within the rubric of the Abraham Accords first brokered by Trump in 2020, normalizing ties with Muslim nations. The United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Morocco are among the countries which have signed the Accords.
Saudi Arabia insists that a prerequisite for it joining the accords is recognition of Palestinian statehood or at least significant progress toward that goal.
Netanyahu, who is now running for re-election, has opposed Palestinian statehood as has his government. Support for two states has plummeted among the Israeli public since the Oct. 7 attacks.
Speaking to reporters earlier today in the Philippines, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the deal, explaining that it was better for Saudi Arabia to build civilian nuclear plants with the United States than with other countries.

sources.news_title: Trump Issues Dual Warnings On Saudi Nuclear Deal And Houthi Ship Attacks
sources.text:
President Donald Trump issued a pair of warnings on Truth Social, first placing a new condition on a civil nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia, then, roughly 20 minutes later, cautioning Iran and its Houthi proxy groups against further attacks on ships in the Red Sea.
Saudi Nuclear Deal Gets a New Condition
In the first post, published at 6:52 a.m. on Thursday morning, Trump focused on a civil nuclear agreement between the U.S. Department of Energy and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Trump wrote that the deal “pertains only to non-military use,” similar to the civil nuclear programs Iran, the UAE, and other countries already have. He added that the deal “will be approved” — but only if Saudi Arabia agrees to join “the very respected and successful Abraham Accords,” the diplomatic effort he started during his first term to build formal ties between Israel and Arab and Muslim-majority nations.
Trump stated that the arrangement would not permit uranium enrichment on Saudi soil, writing, “There will be no enrichment of material!” He closed by stating that “the United States is not opposed to Civil (Non-Enriched) Nuclear Facilities.”
By tying final approval to the Abraham Accords, Trump is reviving a long-standing U.S. demand – that Saudi Arabia improve relations with Israel -V before the nuclear deal can move forward.
What Are the Abraham Accords?
The Abraham Accords are a series of historic normalization agreements brokered by the United States in 2020 during Trump’s first term. They established full diplomatic, economic, and cultural relations between Israel and several Arab and Muslim-majority nations, including the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Sudan, and Morocco.
The accords marked a major shift in Middle East diplomacy by focusing on shared interests like security, trade, and technology rather than resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict first. Trump has frequently described them as one of his signature foreign policy achievements and continues to push for more countries — including Saudi Arabia — to join.
Trump Warns Iran, Houthis Over Red Sea Attacks
In the second post, published at 7:16 a.m., Trump recalled that “a year ago the United States of America attacked, very powerfully, the Houthis” for interfering with maritime commerce and shipping routes by firing at non-military ships. He noted that since that campaign — and throughout the U.S. conflict with Iran — the Yemen-based militant group “have acted very responsibly.”
The President did note that the restraint appears to be ending, pointing to an overnight attack on two Saudi Arabian vessels.
“Unfortunately, now they are starting up again, shooting at two Saudi Arabian ships last night,” Trump wrote. He warned that if the Houthis strike again, the United States “will hold Iran responsible,” describing the group as a “Surrogate and/or Proxy” of Tehran.
"They are starting up again… If they do this again, the U.S. will hold Iran responsible, in that the Houthis are a Surrogate and/or Proxy of Iran, and major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves" – President Donald J. Trump 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/aGLaW6C4nw
— The White House (@WhiteHouse) July 23, 2026
Additionally, Trump said any repeat attack would trigger “major military punishment” against both Iran and the Houthis and added that he was “very disappointed” in the group, which he said had otherwise “acted very professionally and smart” until now.
The President’s warning could be a sign that the U.S. is ready to expand its response beyond Yemen and strike Iran directly if the Houthi groups keep attacking ships.
Two Fronts, One Message
Together, the two posts show Trump applying pressure on two fronts at once – drawing a hard line against Iran and the Houthis in the Red Sea, while using the Saudi nuclear deal as leverage to push Riyadh toward normalizing ties with Israel.
Reactions to Trump’s Posts
Reactions started rolling in within hours of Trump’s posts. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office was among the first to respond in a quick statement, calling a potential Saudi entry into the Abraham Accords “an historic leap forward for peace in the Middle East,” and adding the phrase “Peace through Strength” in support of Trump’s push.
Overseas, France’s Foreign Ministry also weighed in on the Red Sea attacks themselves, calling the Houthi strikes on Saudi tankers “irresponsible and a serious escalation” and urging the group to stand down, per France24.com.

sources.text:
Trump stuns Saudis by pinning nuclear deal to Israel ties
Washington (United States) (AFP) – US President Donald Trump said Thursday that a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia depends on the kingdom recognizing Israel, throwing the agreement into turmoil just the day after it was signed.
Issued on: Modified:
The apparently new condition comes despite Riyadh having long resisted joining the so-called Abraham Accords with Israel, insisting on a pathway to a Palestinian state.
It was not mentioned in the civilian nuclear deal announced on Wednesday, which had appeared to be a major win for the Saudis even as Trump wages war on Iran over its nuclear program.
But Trump stunned the Saudis with his post on his Truth Social network saying the deal "will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords."
The White House insisted that Trump had previously told Saudi Arabia the deal was contingent on recognizing Israel.
"The president is always the final dealmaker. He has said if they don't join the Abraham Accords, the deal is off," Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt told reporters.
"The president has spoken directly with the Saudis about this in numerous conversations in the past, and the administration will continue to engage in those conversations."
'Historic leap'
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said recognition by Saudi Arabia, a regional power and home to Islam's holiest sites, would mark a "historic leap" forward for peace in the Middle East.
Leavitt said she did not know of any calls between Trump and Netanyahu following the announcement of the Saudi agreement.
There was no immediate reaction from Riyadh.
Should it go through, the deal to establish a civilian nuclear program in Saudi Arabia would generate billions of dollars for American companies.
But with Trump's latest announcement, it was unclear whether it would ever see the light of day.
If Washington "tries to force normalization on Riyadh, it's not likely to work out very well," said H.A. Hellyer, senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a leading UK defense and security think tank.
"Would Saudi decide to do a complete 180 on what it has declared for the past three years, or 30 years? Quite dubious," he told AFP.
Critics have also insisted that the deal could precipitate a nuclear race in a region already battered by war.
One provision would potentially see US companies build a uranium enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The US Energy Department made no mention of such a provision and did not offer comment when asked about it by AFP.
And Trump seemingly quashed it by saying on Truth Social that there would be "no enrichment of material!"
The deal will be submitted to Congress for review.
US lawmakers from both parties and Israeli officials have previously voiced opposition to such a project over fears Saudi Arabia could eventually convert it to develop nuclear weapons.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that any civil nuclear agreement signed by Washington with another country "is going to be one that will have safeguards in place to ensure that it can't be turned into a weapons program."
Proliferation concerns
Riyadh, like Tehran, has long been adamant about its right to pursue a civilian nuclear program. Last year it signed a mutual defense pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan.
Policymakers have long feared that if Iran produced a nuclear weapon, the move would set off an arms race across the Gulf.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright dismissed concerns, insisting the deal was in Washington's economic and strategic interest and involved the "highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation."
The United States has agreements governing nuclear cooperation with more than 50 countries.
The Saudi deal meanwhile comes as Riyadh looks set to be dragged further into the Middle East war, with Yemen's Houthi rebels starting to attack ships in the Red Sea to enforce what they say is a blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Trump vowed to punish both Iran and the Houthis if the attacks continue.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Thursday that a new agreement reached with Saudi Arabia for a civilian nuclear program will require the kingdom to normalize relations with Israel through the Abraham Accords.
In a post on social media, the Republican president said the deal does not allow for enrichment of uranium. Nonproliferation experts have raised concerns that the deal fails to include guardrails to prevent enrichment of uranium to weapons-grade levels.
Trump’s post said the agreement “will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords.” He added that the U.S. “is not opposed to Civil (Non-Enriched) Nuclear Facilities.”
The Saudis have made clear that normalizing relations with Israel would first require the establishment of a clear path for Palestinian statehood. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected the idea of Palestinian statehood as being untenable for his country’s security.
The Saudi Embassy in Washington declined to comment Thursday on Trump’s assertion that the deal will require the kingdom to join the accords.
Netanyahu’s office in a statement applauded the prospect of Saudi Arabia joining the accords as a “historic leap forward for peace in the Middle East.” The statement made no mention of the deal to bolster Saudi’s civil nuclear program.
Trump has sought to build on the 2020 agreements, which expanded the number of Arab and Muslim-majority nations with diplomatic ties with Israel. Saudi Arabia is the most important Arab power in the Middle East, and Trump believes the kingdom joining the accords is critical to establishing long-term stability in the region.
The new nuclear deal announced Wednesday is expected to last 30 years and involve U.S. firms in the program’s development. It could allow for the building of a uranium-enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia following a joint U.S.-Saudi study, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The agreement is to be submitted to Congress for review, according to the U.S. and Saudi governments.
The agreement does not include the International Atomic Energy Agency’s “additional protocol,” which would allow for more monitoring, inspections and verification, according to a second person familiar with the decision.
The oil-rich kingdom’s Energy Ministry on Wednesday said the agreement bolsters “efforts to diversify energy sources, advance cutting-edge technologies, and expand opportunities for cooperation and investment in ways that serve the mutual interests of the two friendly countries.”
Enrichment is not an automatic path to a nuclear weapon — a nation also must master other steps, including the use of synchronized high explosives, for instance. But it does open the door to weaponization, which has fueled concerns over Iran’s program.
Administration says deal is good for U.S. firms
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Thursday in Manila that the agreement would make certain that Saudi Arabia works with American companies instead of “competitors” to build its civil nuclear program. China, South Korea, France and Russia are among alternative partners that Riyadh could look to.
“We’re not the only show in town, but we’re the best show in town,” Rubio said. “We want to make sure that it’s our companies they’re picking.”
Trump has talked up his push to extend the Abraham Accords — which also formalized commercial ties between Israel and some Arab and Muslim-majority nations — as key to his plan for bringing long-term stability to the Middle East. But the aftermath of Israel’s war in Gaza and the nearly 5-month-old U.S. and Israel war against Iran have complicated Trump’s push to expand the accords.
The agreements have proven unpopular among the public in certain signatory countries such as Morocco and Bahrain, sparking widespread protests.
Still, the Trump administration remains optimistic that an agreement with Saudi Arabia on joining the accords can be sealed by the end of Trump’s second term.
Deal faces early scrutiny from Congress, Israel and nuclear experts
The White House and Saudi Arabia have not made public the text of the nuclear cooperation agreement, known as a “123 agreement,” alongside what the Trump administration described as a “bilateral safeguards agreement” that was signed Wednesday by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy Abdulaziz bin Salman.
But it already faces scrutiny from Congress, some Israeli officials and nuclear experts.
As details of the deal emerged Wednesday, opposition on Capitol Hill and elsewhere began to snowball, with Republicans and Democrats both questioning the wisdom of the agreement. In addition, conservative commentators who have generally supported Trump’s polices asked why the president would give Saudi Arabia such a deal without getting anything in return.
Then on Thursday, Trump abruptly announced that the deal is entirely contingent on the Saudis joining the accords.
The United Arab Emirates, a neighbor to Saudi Arabia, signed a 123 agreement with the U.S. to build its Barakah nuclear power plant with South Korean assistance. But the UAE did so without seeking enrichment, something nonproliferation experts have held up as the “gold standard” for nations wanting atomic power.
Rubio, as a Republican senator representing Florida, backed a bipartisan 2018 proposal that called for requiring Congress to approve any 123 agreement with Saudi Arabia. The bill was reintroduced by a group of Democratic lawmakers in March but has not passed into law.
Rep. Brad Sherman, a California Democrat, cosponsored with Rubio the 2018 bill that would have required approval from Congress for a nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia. He said he “misses Sen. Rubio,” arguing that Secretary Rubio appears to take a different position.
“I hope that Sen. Rubio will return to us and insist that Congress approve any agreement,” Sherman said Wednesday at a meeting of the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
___
Price reported from Manila, Philippines. Associated Press writers Sam Metz in Jerusalem and Matthew Daly and Matthew Lee in Washington contributed to this report.

Saudi Arabia said the agreement is an effort to diversify energy sources and includes the “highest international standards” of nuclear safety, security, and nonproliferation.

No Israel Recognition, No Nuclear Deal: Trump Sets New Abraham Accords Condition for Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia's nuclear ambitions tied to recognising Israel under Trump's new condition
President Donald Trump has seemingly put Saudi Arabia's long-sought civilian nuclear deal on the line, saying the agreement will only move forward if Riyadh joins the Abraham Accords and recognises Israel.
Trump made the announcement on Truth Social on Thursday, 23 July, just one day after US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement.
'The Civil Nuclear Deal' with Saudi Arabia 'will be approved,' Trump wrote, but added that it is 'totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining' the Abraham Accords.
The statement immediately raised questions about the future of the agreement. The deal had already drawn scrutiny because it could open the door for US companies to help build Saudi Arabia's civilian nuclear energy programme, a project expected to last decades and be worth billions of dollars.
Trump also insisted there would be 'no enrichment of material,' stressing that Washington was not opposed to civilian nuclear facilities as long as they remained non-military.
Why the Saudi Nuclear Deal Is Controversial
The agreement is being described as a 123 agreement, the legal framework the US uses for civil nuclear cooperation with other countries. It gives American companies greater access to Saudi Arabia's planned nuclear energy sector and is expected to be reviewed by Congress. But the details have alarmed nonproliferation experts and Israeli officials.
Reports said the deal does not require Saudi Arabia to sign the International Atomic Energy Agency's Additional Protocol, a stricter inspection system used in other nuclear cooperation agreements. The United Arab Emirates accepted tougher limits in its 2009 nuclear deal with the US, including giving up domestic uranium enrichment.
Enrichment can be used for civilian reactor fuel, but it can also bring a country closer to weapons capability if pushed further. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has previously said the kingdom does not want a nuclear weapon, but he has also warned that Riyadh would pursue one if Iran developed a bomb first.
Abraham Accords Return to the Centre
Trump's new condition revives one of the biggest diplomatic goals of his first term: expanding the Abraham Accords, the normalisation agreements that brought Israel into formal diplomatic relations with several Arab and Muslim-majority states.
The United Arab Emirates and Bahrain joined in 2020, followed by Morocco and Sudan. Saudi Arabia, however, has remained the prize Washington and Israel have long wanted. Riyadh has resisted joining without progress on Palestinian statehood. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected that demand, making the path to normalisation politically difficult.
Trump's post now ties that unresolved diplomatic issue directly to Saudi Arabia's nuclear ambitions.
What Happens Next Post-Agreement
The agreement is not final simply because it was signed. Congress is expected to review it, and lawmakers are likely to examine both the enrichment question and the political condition Trump added after the fact.
The Saudis have not yet publicly accepted Trump's Abraham Accords demand. It is also unclear whether the condition will become a formal legal requirement or remain a presidential red line. For now, the message from Trump is blunt: Saudi Arabia can get a civilian nuclear programme backed by the US, but only if it moves towards recognising Israel.

A civil nuclear agreement between Washington and Riyadh has been under discussion since Trump's first administration and continued under former President Joe Biden, but previous efforts stalled over non-proliferation concerns.

The Abraham Accords are a series of US-brokered agreements launched in 2020 that normalised diplomatic relations between Israel and several Arab countries, including the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco and Sudan.

Trump adds new condition to Saudi nuclear deal, says kingdom must normalize relations with Israel
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday appeared to add a condition to the newly signed agreement with Saudi Arabia for a civilian nuclear program, saying the deal would require the kingdom to normalize its relations with Israel through the Abraham Accords.
When the deal was announced Wednesday, neither the U.S. Energy Department nor the Saudi government made any mention of it being contingent on the kingdom’s relations with Israel.
Trump’s social media post a day later asserting that the agreement was subject to the Saudis joining the accords was unexpected and almost certain to complicate any final approval. The accords approved in 2020 expanded the number of Arab and Muslim-majority nations with diplomatic ties with Israel.
Getting Saudi Arabia to join would be a monumental diplomatic achievement. The Saudis have previously made clear that normalizing relations with Israel would first require the establishment of a clear path for Palestinian statehood. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected the idea of Palestinian statehood as being untenable for his country’s security.
The Republican president also said the pact does not allow for enrichment of uranium. Nonproliferation experts have raised concerns that the deal fails to include guardrails to prevent enrichment of uranium to weapons-grade levels.
Trump said the agreement “will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords.” He added that the U.S. “is not opposed to Civil (Non-Enriched) Nuclear Facilities.”
When asked by a reporter why the condition was not mentioned in the initial announcement, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the president was the “final dealmaker” and has called on Saudi Arabia to join the accords “on numerous occasions.”
The Saudi Embassy in Washington declined to comment Thursday on Trump’s assertions about the deal.
Netanyahu’s office in a statement applauded the prospect of Saudi Arabia joining the accords as a “historic leap forward for peace in the Middle East.” The statement made no mention of the deal to bolster Saudi’s civil nuclear program.
President has sought to build on the accords
Trump has sought to build on the accords, which also formalized commercial ties between Israel and some Arab and Muslim-majority nations. Saudi Arabia is the most important Arab power in the Middle East, and Trump believes the kingdom joining the accords is critical to establishing long-term stability in the region.
The new nuclear deal is expected to last 30 years and involve U.S. firms in the program’s development. The agreement could allow for the building of a uranium-enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia following a joint U.S.-Saudi study, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The pact is to be submitted to Congress for review, according to the U.S. and Saudi governments.
The deal does not include the International Atomic Energy Agency’s “additional protocol,” which would allow for more monitoring, inspections and verification, according to a second person familiar with the agreement.
The oil-rich kingdom’s Energy Ministry on Wednesday said the agreement bolsters “efforts to diversify energy sources, advance cutting-edge technologies, and expand opportunities for cooperation and investment in ways that serve the mutual interests of the two friendly countries.”
Enrichment is not an automatic path to a nuclear weapon — a nation also must master other steps, including the use of synchronized high explosives, for instance. But it does open the door to weaponization, which has fueled concerns over Iran’s program.
Administration says deal is good for US firms
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Thursday in the Philippine capital of Manila that the agreement would make certain that Saudi Arabia works with American companies instead of “competitors” to build its civil nuclear program. China, South Korea, France and Russia are among alternative partners that Riyadh could look to.
“We’re not the only show in town, but we’re the best show in town,” Rubio said. “We want to make sure that it’s our companies they’re picking.”
Trump has talked up his push to extend the accords, but the aftermath of Israel’s war in Gaza and the nearly 5-month-old U.S. and Israel war against Iran have complicated his efforts.
The agreements have proven unpopular in certain signatory countries such as Morocco and Bahrain, sparking widespread protests.
Still, the Trump administration remains optimistic that an agreement with Saudi Arabia on joining the accords can be sealed by the end of Trump’s second term.
Deal faces early scrutiny from Congress, Israel and nuclear experts
The White House and Saudi Arabia have not made public the text of the nuclear cooperation agreement, known as a “123 agreement,” alongside what the Trump administration described as a “bilateral safeguards agreement” that was signed Wednesday by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy Abdulaziz bin Salman.
But it already faces scrutiny from Congress, some Israeli officials and nuclear experts.
As details of the deal emerged Wednesday, opposition on Capitol Hill and elsewhere began to snowball, with Republicans and Democrats both questioning the wisdom of the agreement. In addition, conservative commentators who have generally supported Trump’s polices asked why the president would give Saudi Arabia such a deal without getting anything in return.
Then on Thursday, Trump abruptly announced that the deal is contingent on the Saudis joining the accords.
The United Arab Emirates, a neighbor to Saudi Arabia, signed a 123 agreement with the U.S. to build its Barakah nuclear power plant with South Korean assistance. But the UAE did so without seeking enrichment, something nonproliferation experts have held up as the “gold standard” for nations wanting atomic power.
Rubio, as a Republican senator representing Florida, backed a bipartisan 2018 proposal that called for requiring Congress to approve any 123 agreement with Saudi Arabia. The bill was reintroduced by a group of Democratic lawmakers in March but has not passed into law.

sources.text:
Trump Conditions Saudi Nuclear Deal on Kingdom Joining Abraham Accords
Key Facts
- Trump said the U.S.-Saudi nuclear agreement is contingent upon Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords and normalizing relations with Israel.
- The president insisted the Saudi program must remain civilian and prohibit domestic uranium enrichment.
- Israeli political leaders and nuclear experts warned that insufficient safeguards could fuel a dangerous Middle East arms race.
President says U.S.-backed program must remain civilian and prohibit uranium enrichment as Israeli leaders warn of a regional nuclear arms race
by Emmitt Barry, Worthy News Washington D.C. Bureau Chief
WASHINGTON/JERUSALEM (Worthy News) – President Donald Trump said Thursday that a landmark civilian nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia will move forward only if the kingdom joins the Abraham Accords and formally normalizes relations with Israel.
Trump’s announcement appeared to add a major diplomatic condition to an agreement unveiled one day earlier by the U.S. Department of Energy, which initially made no public mention of Saudi-Israeli normalization.
“The agreement pertains only to non-military use,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that it would be “totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords.”
Trump also said the United States supports civilian nuclear facilities but not Saudi uranium enrichment.
“The United States is not opposed to Civil (Non-Enriched) Nuclear Facilities,” the president wrote.
Decades-Long Nuclear Partnership
The Energy Department announced Wednesday that Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman had signed a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement, commonly known as a Section 123 agreement.
Such agreements are required under the U.S. Atomic Energy Act before significant American nuclear materials, equipment or technology can be transferred to another nation.
The department said the agreement would establish the legal foundation for a “decades-long, multi-billion-dollar partnership” while giving American companies broad access to Saudi Arabia’s emerging nuclear energy industry.
Officials said the arrangement would support American manufacturers, workers and supply chains while helping Saudi Arabia meet its growing domestic energy demands.
The department also said an accompanying safeguards agreement would uphold high standards of nuclear safety, security and nonproliferation. The deal will now be submitted to Congress for review.
Trump’s statement, however, significantly changed the political stakes by tying final approval to what would be one of the most consequential diplomatic breakthroughs in the Middle East: formal peace between Saudi Arabia and Israel.
Questions Over Enrichment and Inspections
The precise limitations contained in the agreement remained a point of dispute Thursday.
Trump explicitly described the proposed Saudi facilities as “non-enriched,” indicating that Riyadh would not be permitted to enrich uranium domestically.
However, Reuters reported that the agreement does not include the full “gold standard” safeguards found in the U.S. nuclear cooperation agreement with the United Arab Emirates. Those standards prohibit domestic uranium enrichment and the reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel.
The agreement also reportedly does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Additional Protocol, which permits more intrusive inspections and expanded verification of nuclear activities.
Those unresolved questions are expected to become a central issue during the congressional review.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has previously warned that the kingdom would seek a nuclear weapon if Iran obtained one—comments that have intensified concerns about transferring sensitive nuclear capabilities to Riyadh.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio sought to calm those fears, saying the United States would not enter into an agreement that creates a proliferation risk.
“The U.S. is not going to reach any agreement with any country in the world that leads to the risk of proliferation,” Rubio said.
Israeli Leaders Warn of Nuclear Arms Race
The agreement quickly drew criticism across Israel’s political spectrum, including from senior opposition leaders and some members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing coalition.
Former Israeli Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman called the prospect of permitting uranium enrichment on Saudi soil “completely unacceptable.”
“Every military nuclear program starts off as a civilian program,” Liberman warned, arguing that the agreement could push the Middle East into “an insane nuclear arms race.”
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett described the deal as a “grave strategic failure” and warned that no government can confidently predict Saudi Arabia’s political direction 10 or 20 years from now.
“What we need is fewer centrifuges in the Middle East, not more,” Bennett said.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid argued that preventing additional nuclear programs in the Middle East is a fundamental responsibility of the Israeli government, while former Defense Minister Benny Gantz said a Saudi civilian nuclear program should be tied to the construction of a broader moderate regional alliance.
Even some members of Netanyahu’s coalition voiced concern.
Heritage Minister Amichay Eliyahu said that while Saudi Arabia may presently be moving in a constructive direction, Israel cannot assume that its policies will remain unchanged indefinitely.
Prime Minister Netanyahu had not publicly commented on the agreement as of Thursday.
Abraham Accords Become Central Condition
Trump has repeatedly called for Saudi Arabia and other Arab and Muslim nations to join the Abraham Accords, which began during his first administration and established formal relations between Israel and several regional governments.
Saudi participation would dramatically expand the accords by bringing the Arab world’s most influential monarchy and the custodian of Islam’s two holiest sites into formal relations with Israel.
Riyadh, however, has maintained that normalization requires meaningful progress toward Palestinian statehood—an issue that remains deeply contested within Israel’s government.
The nuclear agreement now places those competing priorities into a single negotiation: American nuclear technology and long-term strategic cooperation in exchange for Saudi recognition of Israel.
The arrangement could strengthen a regional alliance against Iran, deepen American economic influence in Saudi Arabia and transform Israel’s position in the Arab world. But without enforceable restrictions and credible international inspections, critics warn that the same agreement could introduce another nuclear threshold state into one of the world’s most volatile regions.
Congress will now be tasked with determining whether Trump’s political assurances are fully reflected in the agreement’s legally binding language.

Trump says Saudi nuclear deal subject to forming Israel ties
President Donald Trump said a new civil nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia depends on the kingdom normalizing ties with Israel, a condition that could derail a landmark deal his administration finalized just a day earlier.
In a social media post Thursday, Trump also said there would be “no enrichment” of nuclear material. The pact would allow American companies to expand nuclear energy development in a long-coveted market, but it also raised concerns about a lack of guardrails that would prevent Riyadh from enriching uranium to weapons-grade.
Trump said that the agreement “will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords,” referring to his initiative to get Arab countries to formally recognize Israel.
“The United States is not opposed to Civil (Non-Enriched) Nuclear Facilities,” the president added.
Trump’s surprising demand, coming less than 24 hours after the deal was announced, throws a wrench into its implementation. Saudi Arabia has said it will not normalize ties until Israel accepts Palestinian statehood, something the Israeli government has ruled out.
The full text of the agreement between the Saudis and the U.S. has not been made public, and a U.S. Energy Department statement released Wednesday when the pact was finalized made no mention of Israel or the Abraham Accords.
Saudi Arabia hasn’t commented on Trump’s post.
White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said Thursday she wasn’t aware of any conversations between Trump and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi de facto ruler, since his declaration.
“The president has spoken directly with the Saudis about this in numerous conversations in the past, and the administration will continue to engage in those conversations,” she told reporters. “He has said if they don’t join the Abraham Accords, the deal is off.”
Trump has increased pressure on the kingdom and other countries in the region to join the Abraham Accords. Saudi Arabia is the biggest Arab power in the Middle East and Trump has long desired its participation in order to strengthen the pact and bolster Israel’s long-term security in the region.
“Saudi Arabia’s joining of the Abraham Accords would be an historic leap forward for peace in the Middle East,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said in a statement Thursday.
The prospect of Israel agreeing to Palestinian statehood in the near future is remote, given renewed hostilities in the Middle East following Hamas’s attack on Israel and the subsequent war in Gaza.
The president’s new condition also mirrors the stance of his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, who also sought to link the provision of nuclear technology to the Saudis with normalizing relations with Israel and Israeli concessions to the Palestinians.
The Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel and a subsequent war against the Iran-backed group halted that peacemaking initiative, with Gulf Arab states frequently decrying the violence and death toll in Gaza.
Despite its past misgivings, Israel voiced cautious understanding of Trump’s nuclear accord. Eli Cohen, the Israeli energy minister, said Riyadh might otherwise have sought civilian nuclear capabilities from China, which would have made monitoring them harder. He said Israel’s focus is the potential for future uranium enrichment on Saudi soil.
“It’s our job to worry and to be in dialogue with the Americans,” he told Tel Aviv radio station 103 FM. “On the issue of enrichment: Will it happen? Under what conditions will it happen? Who will have oversight?”
A key part of the Saudi nuclear agreement, likely worth tens of billions of dollars, allows American companies to build a uranium enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia if a study — conducted jointly by the U.S. and the Saudis — determines the move is necessary, according to the Wall Street Journal, which earlier reported on the matter.
The agreement is set to be submitted to Congress, which would need to muster a veto-proof majority to block the measure.
The timing of the accord’s finalization was surprising, given the U.S. is engaged in an active military conflict with Iran designed to destroy Tehran’s nuclear program and prevent the Islamic Republic from acquiring an atomic weapon. Allowing the Saudis to proceed with its own civilian nuclear program alarmed nonproliferation experts worried that it could spark an arms race in the Middle East.

“This is a condition that the president has spoken about many times with our Gulf and Arab allies,” Leavitt said at a White House press briefing, adding: “The president has spoken directly with the Saudis about this in numerous conversations in the past.”
The Abraham Accords are a series of agreements the United States brokered during Trump’s first term in 2020 to establish formal diplomatic, economic and security normalization between several Arab nations and Israel, according to the Middle East Institute. The United Arab Emirates and Bahrain were first to sign the agreements, followed by Morocco.
The Saudis have made clear that normalizing relations with Israel would first require the establishment of a clear path for Palestinian statehood.
Leavitt said she didn’t have any knowledge of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu requesting the Abraham Accords provision for Saudi Arabia. She also said Trump was “the final dealmaker” about the nuclear agreement.

The Trump administration did not release many details about the deal but said the framework could pave the way for the building of a uranium enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia after a joint U.S.-Saudi study, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke with the Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.
“Rest assured, these agreements uphold the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation, while relying on the world’s best nuclear technology and scientists, designed right here in the United States,” Wright said in a statement Wednesday.
The agreement does not include the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Additional Protocol, which would allow for more monitoring, inspections and verification, according to a second person familiar with the decision.
The deal is expected to last 30 years and involve U.S. firms in the program’s development.
On Thursday, Leavitt said the deal “absolutely puts America first, and that’s obviously very important to this president.”
She said the Saudi nuclear energy deal gives priority access to American companies and will benefit American workers.
